extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers seeking information about the Motion Picture Association, its history, and its film content/rating practices
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the Motion Picture Association's historical and current standards for film content (Production Code / 'Don'ts and Be Carefuls') and its voluntary film rating system (CARA/MPA ratings), including procedural practices for review, approval, and enforcement. Useful for understanding what content was/ is considered acceptable and how suitability for audiences is judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Formula (1924 guideline for pre-submission)
rubrics_metrics.description: A loose set of guidelines instituted by Will H. Hays in 1924 that "requested that studios send synopses of films being considered to the MPPDA for review."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to get the industry to self-regulate by pre-screening potential problems; in practice studios were under no obligation to comply and the effort largely failed (studios largely ignored it).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Don'ts and Be Carefuls" (1927 guidance list)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A code of 'Don'ts and Be Carefuls'" created in 1927 outlining issues that movies could encounter in different localities — a list of topics and scenes studios should avoid or treat carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provided examples of problematic material for local censor boards; used as informal guidance rather than enforceable rules (studios often ignored it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Studio Relations Department (SRD) script review/advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Hays created a Studio Relations Department with staff available to studios for script reviews and advice regarding potential problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SRD was meant to provide consultation to help avoid local censorship issues; submission to SRD was voluntary and uptake was limited (by end of 1929 MPPDA received only about 20% of scripts prior to production).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion Picture Production Code (Hays Code) — moral guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduced in 1930, the Motion Picture Production Code (Hays Code) "consisted of moral guidelines regarding what was acceptable to include in films." It incorporated many of the 'Don'ts and Be Carefuls' as specific examples of what could not be portrayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of prohibitions listed in the article: prohibition of "scenes of passion" unless essential to plot; prohibition of "pointed profanity" in word or action; prohibition of "sex perversion"; prohibition of justification or explicit coverage of adultery; prohibition of sympathetic treatment of crime or criminals; prohibition of dancing with "indecent" moves; prohibition of "white slavery" (prostitution). These functioned as content standards for acceptability under the Code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production Code Administration (PCA) — binding approval and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Production Code Administration (PCA), created in response to boycotts, made decisions that were binding; "no film could be exhibited in an American theater without a stamp of approval from the PCA, and any producer attempting to do so faced a fine of $25,000."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under PCA enforcement (from July 1, 1934), PCA rulings were mandatory for theatrical exhibition in the U.S.; the PCA could require edits or refuse approval, effectively vetoing films for exhibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary film ratings system (CARA / Classification and Rating Administration)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1968 Jack Valenti replaced the Production Code with a voluntary film ratings system managed by the Classification and Rating Administration (CARA) to provide parents information about appropriateness of films for children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ratings are voluntary and "have no legal standing." The industry enforces ratings through marketplace practices (e.g., theaters often refuse to exhibit non-rated films). The system is intended to limit censorship while guiding parental choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: G – General Audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: G – General Audiences: "Nothing that would offend parents for viewing by children."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the box: "All ages admitted". Designates material appropriate for all ages; used to indicate no content expected to offend parents for child viewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: PG – Parental Guidance Suggested
rubrics_metrics.description: PG – Parental Guidance Suggested: "Parents urged to give 'parental guidance.' May contain some material parents might not like for their young children."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the box: "Some material may not be suitable for children". Signals that parents should consider content and possibly provide guidance; less restrictive than PG-13 or R.

rubrics_metrics.name: PG-13 – Parents Strongly Cautioned
rubrics_metrics.description: PG-13 – Parents Strongly Cautioned: "Parents are urged to be cautious. Some material may be inappropriate for pre-teenagers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the box: "Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13". Introduced to flag material where parental discretion is more strongly advised than PG.

rubrics_metrics.name: R – Restricted
rubrics_metrics.description: R – Restricted: "Contains some adult material. Parents are urged to learn more about the film before taking their young children with them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the box: "Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian". Industry policy: it is against American film industry policy to admit unaccompanied children to an R-rated film.

rubrics_metrics.name: NC-17 – Adults Only
rubrics_metrics.description: NC-17 – Adults Only: "Clearly adult. Children are not admitted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the box: "No One 17 and Under Admitted". Replaced the 'X' rating in 1990 to denote adult-only content without the pornography connotation of 'X'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratings procedure, transparency, and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: After criticism (e.g., allegations of preferential treatment and lack of transparency), the MPAA posted its ratings rules, policies, procedures, and appeals process online; the article states ratings are "made by an independent group of parents."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The posted rules and appeals process provide procedural guidance for how ratings are assigned and contested; the article notes a CARA-commissioned 2015 study finding high parental approval of the system (93% find it helpful). The appeals process exists but specifics are not enumerated on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry enforcement practices regarding ratings and non-rated films
rubrics_metrics.description: Although ratings are voluntary, the American film industry enforces the MPAA film ratings after assignment: many theaters refuse to exhibit non-rated films, and industry policies restrict admission (e.g., unaccompanied children to R films).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences of lacking or receiving a restrictive rating include limited exhibition opportunities and marketplace pressure to edit or appeal ratings; an unrated film is often denoted by "NR" in listings though this is not a formal MPAA rating.
